titles.Paracortex: T-cell zone and high endothelial venules

Capsule & trabeculae.description: The capsule is a sheath of dense irregular connective tissue, rich in collagen, that encloses the whole node. Trabeculae are connective-tissue septa that run inward from the capsule, carry blood vessels and partly divide the cortex into compartments.
clinical: Cancer that breaks through the nodal capsule is called extranodal extension. Pathologists record it because it is an adverse prognostic feature, for example in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

Hilum & vessels.description: The hilum is the indentation on the concave side where the nodal artery enters and the vein and efferent lymphatic vessel leave; it is packed with connective tissue and fat that continues from the capsule. The artery branches through the trabeculae and medulla into capillary beds, and blood drains through postcapillary venules, including the high endothelial venules of the paracortex.
clinical: On ultrasound or CT, a node that loses its fatty hilum and becomes rounder is more likely to be abnormal, whether the cause is reactive or malignant.

Sinuses.description: Lymph flows from the afferent vessels into the subcapsular sinus, then along the trabecular sinuses through the cortex to the medullary sinuses. The sinuses are lined by endothelium and crossed by reticular fibres, and sinus macrophages trap particles and microbes as the lymph filters past them.
clinical: Cancer cells carried in afferent lymph are often first caught in the subcapsular sinus, so early deposits of metastatic cancer are commonly seen there.

Cortex.description: The outer cortex is the B-cell zone: round follicles of densely packed naive B cells sit on a meshwork of follicular dendritic cells, with diffuse lymphoid tissue between them. After antigen stimulation a follicle becomes a secondary follicle, with a germinal centre whose dark zone holds dividing, mutating B cells and whose light zone selects B cells with higher-affinity antigen receptors, surrounded by a mantle of naive B cells.
clinical: Follicular lymphoma is a cancer of germinal-centre B cells, most often with the t(14;18) translocation that over-expresses BCL2.
After viral infection or other antigen stimulation, germinal centres enlarge and multiply, a common reactive pattern in lymph nodes.

Paracortex.description: The paracortex, or deep cortex, is the T-cell zone that lies between the follicles and the medulla. Dendritic cells arriving in afferent lymph present antigen to T cells here, and naive lymphocytes enter the node from the blood through the high endothelial venules that line this region.
clinical: Infectious mononucleosis, caused by Epstein-Barr virus, makes the paracortex expand with large immunoblasts, so the node can look like lymphoma.

Medulla.description: The medulla contains branching medullary cords of lymphoid tissue, rich in plasma cells, macrophages and lymphocytes, that continue from the paracortex. Plasma cells in the cords secrete antibody into the lymph leaving the node.
clinical: A medulla crowded with plasma cells is a reactive pattern seen with long-standing antigen stimulation, such as chronic infection or autoimmune disease.

Lymphatics.description: Afferent lymphatic vessels are thin-walled collecting vessels that pierce the capsule on the convex surface and empty into the subcapsular sinus, with valves that keep lymph flowing one way. The efferent vessel, usually just one, leaves at the hilum and carries filtered lymph, plasma-cell antibody and activated lymphocytes toward the next node in the chain or the main lymph trunks.
clinical: Blocked or removed lymph drainage causes lymphoedema, for example in the arm after axillary node clearance for breast cancer.
Cancer reaches a node through its afferent lymphatics, which is why sentinel node biopsy follows the lymph drainage of a tumour.

parts.description: The capsule is the tough outer shell of the lymph node, a sheath of dense irregular connective tissue rich in collagen that encloses the whole organ. It is continuous with the connective tissue of the hilum, and the trabeculae project inward from it. In a stained section it appears as a pink, fibrous band at the outer edge of the node, separating the lymphoid tissue from the surrounding fat.

Trabeculae are fibrous septa, or partitions, that extend inward from the capsule into the cortex and medulla of the lymph node. They carry blood vessels into the node and partly divide the lymphoid tissue into compartments. In a section they appear as thin bands of dense collagen running from the capsule into the tissue, with small vessels and fibroblasts within them.

Hilum connective tissue is the fibrous and fatty tissue that fills the hilum, the concave indentation on one side of the lymph node. It is continuous with the capsule and surrounds the nodal artery, vein and efferent lymphatic vessel where they enter and leave. In a section it appears as loose connective tissue with fat cells at the concave border, where the vessels pass in and out of the node.

The subcapsular sinus is the first lymph channel inside the node, a narrow space lying between the capsule and the outer cortex. Afferent lymph enters it from the afferent lymphatic vessels and then drains into the trabecular sinuses that run through the cortex. In a section it appears as a pale gap beneath the capsule, lined by flattened endothelial and reticular cells, crossed by reticular fibres and dotted with sinus macrophages.

The trabecular sinuses are lymph channels that run through the cortex alongside the trabeculae, linking the subcapsular sinus with the medullary sinuses. They lie in the connective tissue that accompanies each trabecula, so lymph passes deep into the node between the follicles. In a section they look like pale, irregular spaces along the trabeculae, with sinus macrophages and reticular fibres crossing the lumen.

The outer cortex is the superficial layer of the lymph node cortex, lying just beneath the subcapsular sinus, and it is the B-cell zone. It contains the lymphoid follicles, dense spherical masses of B lymphocytes held in a meshwork of reticular fibres and follicular dendritic cells. In a stained section it appears as a band of closely packed, darkly stained round nodules.

Primary follicles are small, round aggregates of naive B lymphocytes that lie in the outer cortex. They have no germinal centre, so they appear as uniformly dense, dark-staining spheres of small lymphocytes supported by follicular dendritic cells. A primary follicle is the resting form of a lymphoid follicle; after antigen stimulation it develops a germinal centre and becomes a secondary follicle.

The mantle zone is the dense ring of small, naive B lymphocytes that surrounds the germinal centre of a secondary follicle. It sits between the germinal centre and the surrounding cortex, and acts as a reservoir of unstimulated B cells that can respond to antigen and move into the germinal centre. In a section it appears as a dark crown of small round cells encircling the paler germinal centre.

keys: Anterior cover: Germinal centre - light zone
parts.description: The light zone of a germinal centre is its paler part, where B cells compete for antigen held on follicular dendritic cells. Its cells are less tightly packed than in the dark zone and include centrocytes (the smaller B cells undergoing selection), helper T cells and macrophages that clear dead cells. This is where B cells with higher-affinity antigen receptors are selected, and in a section the zone looks paler because its cells are more loosely packed.

keys: Anterior cover: Germinal centre - dark zone
parts.description: The dark zone of a germinal centre is the densely packed region of rapidly dividing B cells called centroblasts. In this zone the antibody genes of these cells undergo somatic hypermutation, a rapid, random change in the antigen-binding part of the gene, which creates variant receptors for selection. In a section the dark zone looks darker than the light zone because of its crowded nuclei and many dividing cells.

High endothelial venules are postcapillary venules, the small veins that collect blood from capillaries, found in the paracortex. Their wall is lined by unusually tall, cuboidal endothelial cells, and they are the main route by which naive lymphocytes leave the blood and enter the lymph node. Lymphocytes roll along the lining and squeeze through it, so in a section the venules are recognised by their plump, high endothelium and the lymphocytes packed in or near their lumen.

The medullary sinuses are the lymph channels of the medulla, lying between the medullary cords. They receive lymph from the trabecular sinuses and carry it toward the hilum, where it leaves the node through the efferent lymphatic vessel. In a section they appear as pale, open spaces between the darker cords of lymphoid tissue, containing sinus macrophages and a few lymphocytes.

The reticular fibre meshwork is the fine supporting framework of the lymph node, made of thin reticular fibres of type III collagen laid down by fibroblastic reticular cells, the node's own connective-tissue cells. It runs through the cortex, paracortex and medulla, holding the lymphocytes in place and crossing the sinuses so that lymph can filter through them. In a section it is best seen with a silver stain, which turns the fibres black against the lymphoid background.

Sinus macrophages are large cells that engulf particles and microbes by phagocytosis, and they lie along the lymph sinuses. They attach to the reticular fibres that cross the sinus lumen and trap bacteria, particles and cell debris as lymph filters past them, and some pass antigen to nearby lymphocytes. In a section they appear as large cells with pale, foamy cytoplasm, sometimes containing dark ingested material.

Afferent lymphatic vessels are the thin-walled channels that carry lymph, together with antigen-bearing dendritic cells, into the node from the tissues. Several of them pierce the capsule on the convex surface and open into the subcapsular sinus, and valves inside them keep the lymph flowing one way. In a section they look like small, thin-walled vessels close to the capsule on the convex side of the node.

The efferent lymphatic vessel is the lymph vessel that leaves the node at the hilum, usually as a single vessel. It carries filtered lymph, along with antibodies from plasma cells and activated lymphocytes, out of the node toward the next lymph node in the chain or the main lymphatic trunks. Because it leaves at the hilum, it lies beside the nodal artery and vein, and in a section it is recognised by its thin wall and its position there.

Lymphatic valves are paired, cusp-like folds of the lining of lymphatic vessels, found inside the afferent and efferent vessels of the node. Their cusps point in the direction of lymph flow, so they stop lymph from flowing backwards when the vessel is squeezed or relaxes. In a section a valve appears as a small inward fold of the endothelium, and the vessel looks slightly swollen at that point.

keys: Anterior cover: Artery (hilar and medullary branches)
parts.description: The hilar and medullary arteries are the branches of the nodal artery that supply the lymph node with blood. The nodal artery enters at the hilum, and its branches run through the hilar fat, the trabeculae and the medulla, feeding capillary beds that nourish the lymphoid tissue. In a section they are recognised by their thick, muscular wall and round lumen, which set them apart from the thin-walled veins and lymphatic channels.

keys: Anterior cover: Vein (hilar and medullary tributaries)
parts.description: The hilar and medullary veins are the blood vessels that drain the lymph node, collecting blood from its capillary beds and postcapillary venules. Their tributaries run through the medulla and trabeculae and join the nodal vein at the hilum, which leaves the node alongside the efferent lymphatic vessel. In a section the veins have a thinner wall and a wider, often collapsed lumen than the nodal arteries.
